title: Episode 7 — Aeolus
paragraphs: IN THE HEART OF THE HIBERNIAN METROPOLIS

In front of Nelson's Pillar, trams slowed down, switched tracks, changed their trolley poles, and set off for Blackrock, Kingstown and Dalkey, Clonskea, Rathgar and Terenure, Palmerston Park and upper Rathmines, Sandymount Green, Rathmines, Ringsend and Sandymount Tower, Harold's Cross. The hoarse Dublin United Tramway Company timekeeper shouted them off:
—Rathgar and Terenure!
—Come on, Sandymount Green!
To the right and left, clanging and ringing in parallel, a double-decker and a single-decker moved from their starting points, swerved to the down line, and glided along side by side.
—Start, Palmerston Park!
THE WEARER OF THE CROWN

Under the porch of the General Post Office, shoeshine boys called out and polished boots. Parked in North Prince's Street, His Majesty's bright red mail cars, bearing the royal initials E.R. on their sides, received loudly flung sacks of letters, postcards, letter-cards, parcels, insured and paid, for local, provincial, British, and overseas delivery.
GENTLEMEN OF THE PRESS

Heavy-booted draymen rolled barrels out of Prince's stores with dull thuds and bumped them up onto the brewery wagon. On the brewery wagon, dull-thudding barrels were rolled by heavy-booted draymen out of Prince's stores.
—There it is, Red Murray said. Alexander Keyes.
—Just cut it out, will you? Mr Bloom said, and I'll take it round to the _Telegraph_ office.

The door of Ruttledge's office creaked again. Davy Stephens, a tiny figure in a large cape-coat, a small felt hat crowning his ringlets, passed out with a roll of papers under his cape, like a king's courier.
Red Murray's long shears sliced the advertisement out of the newspaper in four clean strokes. Scissors and paste.
—I'll go through the printing works, Mr Bloom said, taking the cut-out square.
—Of course, if he wants a paragraph, Red Murray said earnestly, a pen behind his ear, we can write him one.
—Right, Mr Bloom said with a nod. I'll push that idea.
We.
WILLIAM BRAYDEN, ESQUIRE, OF OAKLANDS, SANDYMOUNT
Red Murray touched Mr Bloom's arm with the shears and whispered:
—Brayden.

Mr Bloom turned and saw the uniformed porter raise his lettered cap as a stately figure entered between the newsboards of the _Weekly Freeman and National Press_ and the _Freeman's Journal and National Press_. The dull thudding of Guinness's barrels. The figure passed grandly up the staircase, steered by an umbrella, a solemn beard-framed face. The broadcloth back ascended each step: back. All his brains are in the back of his neck, Simon Dedalus says. Rolls of flesh behind him. Fat folds of neck, fat, neck, fat, neck.
—Don't you think his face looks like Our Saviour? Red Murray whispered.
The door of Ruttledge's office whispered: ee: cree. They always build one door opposite another so the wind can blow through. Way in. Way out.
Our Saviour: beard-framed oval face: talking in the twilight. Mary, Martha. Steered by an umbrella-sword to the footlights: Mario the tenor.
—Or like Mario, Mr Bloom said.
—Yes, Red Murray agreed. But Mario was said to be the image of Our Saviour.
Jesus-Mario with rouged cheeks, doublet, and spindle legs. Hand on his heart. In the opera _Martha._

Co-ome thou lost one,
     Co-ome thou dear one!
THE CROZIER AND THE PEN
—His Grace phoned down twice this morning, Red Murray said gravely.
They watched the knees, legs, boots vanish. Neck.
A telegram boy stepped in nimbly, threw an envelope on the counter, and stepped off in a hurry with a word:
_—Freeman!_
Mr Bloom said slowly:
—Well, he is one of our saviours also.

A meek smile went with him as he lifted the counter flap, as he passed through a side door and along the warm dark stairs and passage, along the now vibrating boards. But will he save the circulation? Thumping. Thumping.
He pushed through the glass swing door and entered, stepping over scattered packing paper. Through a lane of clanking drums he made his way towards Nannetti's reading closet.
WITH UNFEIGNED REGRET IT IS WE ANNOUNCE THE DISSOLUTION OF A MOST RESPECTED DUBLIN BURGESS

Hynes here too: account of the funeral probably. Thumping. Thump. This morning the remains of the late Mr Patrick Dignam. Machines. They'd smash a man to atoms if he got caught in them. They rule the world today. His bodily machinery is working away too. Like these, got out of hand: fermenting. Working away, tearing away. And that old grey rat tearing to get in.
HOW A GREAT DAILY ORGAN IS TURNED OUT
Mr Bloom halted behind the foreman's thin body, admiring a glossy bald crown.

Strange he never saw his real country. Ireland my country. Member of Parliament for College Green. He milked that common-man worker angle for all it was worth. It's the ads and special features that sell a weekly paper, not the stale news in the official gazette. Queen Anne is dead. Published by authority in the year one thousand and. Property situated in the township of Rosenallis, barony of Tinnahinch. To all whom it may concern: schedule pursuant to statute showing return of number of mules and donkeys exported from Ballina. Nature notes. Cartoons. Phil Blake's weekly Pat and Bull story. Uncle Toby's page for tiny tots. Country bumpkin's queries. Dear Mr Editor, what is a good cure for flatulence? I'd enjoy that section. You learn a lot by teaching others. The personal column. M.A.P. Mainly all pictures. Shapely bathers on golden strand. World's biggest balloon. Double marriage of sisters celebrated. Two bridegrooms laughing heartily at each other. Nannetti too, an Italian-Irish printer. More Irish than the Irish.

The machines clanked in three-four time. Thump, thump, thump. Now if he had a stroke right there and no one knew how to stop the machines, they'd clank on and on, printing the same thing over and over, up and back. Make a mess of the whole thing. Need a cool head.
—Well, get it into the evening edition, councillor, Hynes said.
They'll be calling him lord mayor soon. Long John Fanning is backing him, they say.
The foreman, without answering, scribbled 'press' on a corner of the sheet and made a sign to a typesetter. He handed the sheet silently over the dirty glass screen.
—Right: thanks, Hynes said, moving off.
Mr Bloom stood in his way.
—If you want to collect your pay, the cashier is just going to lunch, he said, pointing backward with his thumb.
—Did you? Hynes asked.
—Mm, Mr Bloom said. Look sharp and you'll catch him.
—Thanks, old man, Hynes said. I'll hit him up too.
He hurried on eagerly towards the _Freeman's Journal_.
Three shillings I lent him at Meagher's. Three weeks ago. Third hint I've dropped.
WE SEE THE CANVASSER AT WORK
Mr Bloom laid his cutting on Mr Nannetti's desk.
—Excuse me, councillor, he said. This ad, you see. Keyes, you remember?
Mr Nannetti considered the cutting for a while and nodded.
—He wants it in for July, Mr Bloom said.
The foreman moved his pencil towards it.
—But wait, Mr Bloom said. He wants it changed. Keyes, you see. He wants two keys at the top.
Hell of a racket these machines make. He doesn't even hear it. Nannetti. Iron nerves. Maybe he understands what I'm getting at.
The foreman turned round to listen patiently and, lifting an elbow, began to scratch slowly in the armpit of his alpaca jacket.
—Like that, Mr Bloom said, crossing his forefingers at the top.
Let him take that in first.

Mr Bloom, glancing sideways up from the cross shape he had made with his fingers, saw the foreman's sallow face — looks like he has a touch of jaundice — and beyond him the obedient reels feeding in huge webs of paper. Clank it. Clank it. Miles of it unreeled. What becomes of it afterwards? Oh, wrap up meat, parcels: various uses, a thousand and one things.
Slipping his words deftly into the pauses between the clanking, Bloom drew swiftly on the scarred woodwork.
HOUSE OF KEY(E)S
—Like that, see. Two crossed keys here. A circle. Then here the name. Alexander Keyes, tea, wine, and spirit merchant. And so on.
Better not teach him his own business.
—You know yourself, councillor, just what he wants. Then round the top in bold type: the house of keys. You see? Do you think that's a good idea?
The foreman moved his scratching hand to his lower ribs and scratched there quietly.

—The idea, Mr Bloom said, is the House of Keys. You know, councillor, the Manx parliament. A hint at home rule for Ireland. Tourists, you know, from the Isle of Man. Catches the eye, you see. Can you do that?
I could ask him perhaps about how to pronounce that Italian word _voglio_. But then if he didn't know, it would only make things awkward for him. Better not.
—We can do that, the foreman said. Have you the design?

—I can get it, Mr Bloom said. It was in a Kilkenny paper. He has a house there too. I'll just run out and ask him. Well, you can do that and just a little paragraph calling attention. You know the usual. High-class licensed premises. Long-felt want. And so on.
The foreman thought for an instant.
—We can do that, he said. Let him give us a three months' renewal.
A typesetter brought him a limp galley proof. He began to check it silently. Mr Bloom stood by, hearing the loud throbs of cranks, watching the silent typesetters at their cases.
ORTHOGRAPHICAL

Wants to be sure of his spelling. Proofreading fever. Martin Cunningham forgot to give us his spelling bee puzzle this morning. It is amusing to view the unpar-one-ar-alleled embarra-two-ars-is-it? double-ess-ment of a harassed pedlar while gauging the symmetry-with-a-y of a peeled pear under a cemetery wall. Silly, isn't it? Cemetery put in of course because it rhymes with symmetry.

I should have said something when he put on his top hat. Thank you. I ought to have said something about an old hat or something. No. I could have said: Looks as good as new now. Should have seen the look on his face then.

Sllt. The bottom deck of the first machine jogged forward its flyboard with sllt the first batch of folded papers. Sllt. Almost human the way it goes sllt to call attention. Doing its level best to speak. That door too — sllt — creaking, asking to be shut. Everything speaks in its own way. Sllt.
NOTED CHURCHMAN AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR
The foreman handed back the galley proof suddenly, saying:
—Wait. Where's the archbishop's letter? It's to be reprinted in the _Telegraph._ Where's what's his name?
He looked around at his loud, unanswering machines.
—Monks, sir? a voice asked from the casting box.
—Yes. Where's Monks?
—Monks!
Mr Bloom took up his cutting. Time to get out.
—Then I'll get the design, Mr Nannetti, he said, and you'll give it a good place, I know.
—Monks!
—Yes, sir.
Three months' renewal. Want to get this off my chest first. Try it anyway. Push the August angle: good idea — horse show month. Ballsbridge. Tourists over for the show.
A DAYFATHER

He walked on through the composing room, passing an old man, stooped, spectacled, wearing an apron. Old Monks, the day-shift supervisor. Strange lot of stuff he must have handled in his time: obituary notices, pub ads, speeches, divorce cases, found drowned. Nearing the end of his working life now. Sensible, serious man with a bit saved in the bank, I'd say. Wife a good cook and laundress. Daughter working the sewing machine in the parlour. Plain Jane, no damn nonsense.
AND IT WAS THE FEAST OF THE PASSOVER

He paused in his walk to watch a typesetter neatly distributing type. Reads it backwards first. Quickly he does it. Must take some practice, that. mangiD kcirtaP — Patrick Dignam spelled backwards. Poor Papa with his Haggadah book, reading backwards with his finger for me. Passover. Next year in Jerusalem. Dear, oh dear! All that long business about how God brought us out of the land of Egypt and into the house of bondage. _Alleluia. Shema Israel Adonai Elohenu_. No, that's a different prayer. Then the twelve brothers, Jacob's sons. And then the lamb and the cat and the dog and the stick and the water and the butcher. And then the angel of death kills the butcher and he kills the ox and the dog kills the cat. Sounds a bit silly until you look into it properly. It means justice, but it's everybody eating everyone else. That's what life is, after all. How quickly he does that job. Practice makes perfect. Seems to see with his fingers.

Mr Bloom passed on out of the clanking noises through the gallery onto the landing. Now am I going to take the tram all the way out there and then maybe miss him? Better phone him first. Number? Yes. Same as Citron's house. Twenty-eight. Twenty-eight double four.
ONLY ONCE MORE THAT SOAP

He went down the staircase. Who the devil scrawled all over those walls with matches? Looks as if they did it for a bet. There's always a heavy greasy smell in those works. Lukewarm glue in Thom's next door when I was there.

He took out his handkerchief to dab his nose. Lemon-citron? Ah, the soap I put there. I'll lose it from that pocket. Putting back his handkerchief, he took out the soap and stowed it away, buttoned, into the hip pocket of his trousers.
What perfume does your wife use? I could still go home: take the tram: something I forgot. Just to see: before: dressing. No. Here. No.
A sudden screech of laughter came from the _Evening Telegraph_ office. I know who that is. What's going on? I'll pop in for a minute to use the phone. It's Ned Lambert.
He entered softly.
ERIN, GREEN GEM OF THE SILVER SEA
—The boss is here — payday, Professor MacHugh murmured softly, crumblingly, to the dusty windowpane.
Mr Dedalus, staring from the empty fireplace at Ned Lambert's amused face, asked sourly:
—Christ almighty, wouldn't it give you heartburn on your arse?
Ned Lambert, seated on the table, read on:

—_Or again, note the meanderings of some babbling brook as it chatters on its way, though quarrelling with the stony obstacles, to the tumbling waters of Neptune's blue domain, amid mossy banks, fanned by the gentlest breezes, played on by the glorious sunlight or beneath the shadows cast over its pensive surface by the overarching foliage of the forest giants._ What about that, Simon? he asked over the edge of his newspaper. How's that for grand style?
—He must have switched his drink, Mr Dedalus said.
Ned Lambert, laughing, struck the newspaper on his knees, repeating:
—_The pensive surface and the overarsing foliage_. Oh boys! Oh boys!
—And Xenophon looked upon Marathon, Mr Dedalus said, looking again at the fireplace and to the window, and Marathon looked on the sea.
—That will do, Professor MacHugh cried from the window. I don't want to hear any more of that rubbish.
He ate the crescent-shaped piece of water biscuit he had been nibbling and, still hungry, made ready to nibble the biscuit in his other hand.

Highfalutin stuff. Windbags. Ned Lambert is taking a day off, I see. A funeral rather throws off a man's day. He has influence, they say. Old Chatterton, the vice-chancellor, is his granduncle or great-granduncle. Close to ninety, they say. His obituary probably already written and waiting. Living just to spite them. Might die first himself. Make room for your uncle, Johnny. The Right Honourable Hedges Eyre Chatterton. I'd guess he writes him the odd shaky cheque on quarter days. Nice windfall when the old man kicks the bucket. Alleluia.
—Just one more bit, Ned Lambert said.
—What is it? Mr Bloom asked.
—A recently discovered fragment of Cicero, Professor MacHugh answered with a pompous tone. _Our lovely land._
SHORT BUT TO THE POINT
—Whose land? Mr Bloom said simply.
—Most pertinent question, the professor said between his chews. With an accent on the _whose_.
—Dan Dawson's land, Mr Dedalus said.
—Is it his speech from last night? Mr Bloom asked.
Ned Lambert nodded.
—But listen to this, he said.
The doorknob hit Mr Bloom in the small of the back as the door was pushed open.
—Excuse me, J. J. O'Molloy said, entering.
Mr Bloom moved nimbly aside.
—I beg your pardon, he said.
—Good day, Jack.
—Come in. Come in.
—Good day.
—How are you, Dedalus?
—Well. And yourself?
J. J. O'Molloy shook his head.
SAD
Used to be the cleverest fellow at the junior bar. Going downhill, poor chap. That feverish flush spells the end for a man. Touch and go with him. What's he after, I wonder. Money trouble.
—_Or again if we but climb the serried mountain peaks._
—You're looking well.
—Is the editor in? J. J. O'Molloy asked, looking towards the inner door.
—Very much so, Professor MacHugh said. To be seen and heard. He's in his office with Lenehan.
J. J. O'Molloy strolled to the sloping desk and began to turn back the pink pages of the file.

His practice is dwindling. A might-have-been. Losing heart. Gambling. Debts of honour. Reaping the whirlwind. Used to get good fees from D. and T. Fitzgerald. Those barristers in their wigs, showing off their grey matter. Brains on their sleeve, like the statue in Glasnevin cemetery. I believe he does some literary work for the _Express_ with Gabriel Conroy. Well-read fellow. Myles Crawford started at the _Independent_. Funny the way those newspaper men shift allegiance when they smell a new opportunity. Weathervanes. Hot and cold in the same breath. You wouldn't know which to believe. One story sounds good till you hear the next. They go at each other hammer and tongs in the papers and then it all blows over. Best mates the next moment.
—Ah, listen to this for God's sake, Ned Lambert pleaded. _Or again if we but climb the serried mountain peaks..._
—Bombast! the professor broke in testily. Enough of the inflated windbag!
—_Peaks_, Ned Lambert went on, _towering high on high, to bathe our souls, as it were..._
—He should wash his mouth out, Mr Dedalus said. Blessed and eternal God! Yes? Is he taking anything for it?

_—As it were, in the peerless panorama of Ireland's finest scenery, unmatched, despite their well-praised counterparts in other celebrated regions, for sheer beauty — of leafy groves and rolling plains and lush green pastureland, steeped in the transcendent, translucent glow of our mild, mysterious Irish twilight..._
HIS NATIVE DORIC
—The moon, Professor MacHugh said. He forgot Hamlet.
_—That spreads across the vista far and wide, and wait till the glowing orb of the moon shines forth to bathe everything in its silver radiance..._
—Oh! Mr Dedalus cried, letting out a hopeless groan. Shit and onions! That'll do, Ned. Life is too short.
He took off his silk hat and, blowing out impatiently past his bushy moustache, combed his hair with raking fingers.
Ned Lambert tossed the newspaper aside, chuckling with delight. An instant later a hoarse bark of laughter burst over Professor MacHugh's unshaven, black-spectacled face.
—Doughy Daw! he cried.
WHAT WETHERUP SAID

Easy enough to mock it now in cold print, but that stuff goes down a treat with audiences. He was in the baking business too, wasn't he? That's why they call him Doughy Daw. Feathered his nest well enough, anyway. Daughter engaged to that fellow in the tax office who has a motor car. Landed that nicely. Entertaining. Open house. Big blowout parties. Wetherup always said that. Win them over through their stomachs.
The inner door was flung open violently and a scarlet, beak-like face, topped by a comb of feathery hair, thrust itself in. The bold blue eyes stared around and the harsh voice asked:
—What is it?
—And here comes the sham squire himself! Professor MacHugh said grandly.
—Get out of that, you bloody old schoolteacher! the editor said in greeting.
—Come, Ned, Mr Dedalus said, putting on his hat. I must get a drink after that.
—Drink! the editor cried. No drinks served before mass.
—Quite right too, Mr Dedalus said, going out. Come on, Ned.
Ned Lambert slid down from the table. The editor's blue eyes roved towards Mr Bloom's face, shadowed by a smile.
—Will you join us, Myles? Ned Lambert asked.
MEMORABLE BATTLES RECALLED
—North Cork militia! the editor cried, striding to the mantelpiece. We won every time! North Cork and Spanish officers!
—Where was that, Myles? Ned Lambert asked with a reflective glance at his shoes.
—In Ohio! the editor shouted.
—So it was, by God, Ned Lambert agreed.
Passing out, he whispered to J. J. O'Molloy:
—He's losing it. Sad case.
—Ohio! the editor crowed in high-pitched tones from his upturned scarlet face. My Ohio!
—A perfect cretic metre! the professor said. Long, short, and long.
O, HARP EOLIAN!
He took a reel of dental floss from his waistcoat pocket and, breaking off a piece, twanged it smartly between two and two of his unclean, resonant teeth.
—Bingbang, bangbang.
Mr Bloom, seeing the coast was clear, headed for the inner door.
—Just a moment, Mr Crawford, he said. I just want to phone about an ad.
He went in.
—What about that editorial piece this evening? Professor MacHugh asked, coming to the editor and laying a firm hand on his shoulder.
—That'll be all right, Myles Crawford said more calmly. Don't you worry. Hello, Jack. That's all right.
—Good day, Myles, J. J. O'Molloy said, letting the pages he held slip limply back onto the file. Is that Canada swindle case on today?
The telephone whirred inside.
—Twenty-eight... No, twenty... Double four... Yes.
SPOT THE WINNER
Lenehan came out of the inner office with the racing pages from _Sport_.
—Who wants a sure thing for the Gold Cup? he asked. Sceptre with O. Madden riding.
He tossed the pages onto the table.
Screams of barefoot newsboys in the hall rushed nearer and the door was flung open.
—Shh, Lenehan said. I hear footsteps.

Professor MacHugh strode across the room and seized the cringing urchin by the collar as the others scampered out of the hall and down the steps. The racing pages rustled up in the draught, floated softly through the air, blue scrawls, and drifted under the table to the floor.
—It wasn't me, sir. It was the big fellow who shoved me, sir.
—Throw him out and shut the door, the editor said. There's a hurricane blowing.
Lenehan began to gather the pages up from the floor, grunting as he stooped twice.
—Waiting for the racing special, sir, the newsboy said. It was Pat Farrell shoved me, sir.
He pointed to two faces peering in round the doorframe.
—Him, sir.
—Out of here with you, Professor MacHugh said gruffly.
He hustled the boy out and banged the door shut.
J. J. O'Molloy turned the files over with a crackling sound, murmuring, searching:
—Continued on page six, column four.
—Yes, _Evening Telegraph_ here, Mr Bloom phoned from the inner office. Is the boss...? Yes, _Telegraph_... Where? Aha! Which auction rooms?... Aha! I see... Right. I'll catch him.
A COLLISION ENSUES
The bell whirred again as he hung up. He came out quickly and bumped into Lenehan, who was struggling up with the second racing page.
—_Pardon, monsieur_, Lenehan said, clutching him for an instant and making a face.
—My fault, Mr Bloom said, enduring his grip. Are you hurt? I'm in a hurry.
—Knee, Lenehan said.
He made a comic face and whined, rubbing his knee:
—The wear and tear of the years.
—Sorry, Mr Bloom said.

He went to the door and, holding it ajar, paused. J. J. O'Molloy flipped the heavy pages over. The noise of two shrill voices and a harmonica echoed in the bare hallway from the newsboys squatting on the doorsteps:

We are the boys of Wexford
     Who fought with heart and hand.
EXIT BLOOM
—I'm just running round to Bachelor's Walk, Mr Bloom said, about this ad of Keyes's. Want to get it sorted. They tell me he's round there in Dillon's.
He looked indecisively for a moment at their faces. The editor, who had been leaning against the mantelshelf with his head propped on his hand, suddenly stretched forth an arm grandly.
—Begone! he said. The world is before you.
—Back in no time, Mr Bloom said, hurrying out.
J. J. O'Molloy took the racing pages from Lenehan's hand and read them, blowing them apart gently, without comment.
—He'll get that advertisement, the professor said, staring through his black-rimmed spectacles over the half-blind. Look at the young rascals chasing after him.
—Show. Where? Lenehan cried, running to the window.
A STREET CORTÈGE
Both smiled over the half-blind at the file of capering newsboys in Mr Bloom's wake, the last one zigzagging a white paper on the breeze like a mocking kite, a tail of white bow-knots.
—Look at the young guttersnipe behind him in hot pursuit, Lenehan said, and you'll die laughing. Oh, my ribs! Imitating his flat feet and his walk. The little runt. Cheeky as anything.
He began to dance in swift caricature across the floor on sliding feet, past the fireplace, to J. J. O'Molloy, who placed the racing pages in his receiving hands.
—What's that? Myles Crawford said with a start. Where are the other two gone?
—Who? the professor said, turning. They've gone round to the Oval for a drink. Paddy Hooper is there with Jack Hall. Came over last night.
—Come on then, Myles Crawford said. Where's my hat?
He walked jerkily into the office behind, parting the vent of his jacket, jingling his keys in his back pocket. They jingled in the air and against the wood as he locked his desk drawer.
—He's fairly drunk, Professor MacHugh said in a low voice.
—Seems to be, J. J. O'Molloy said, taking out a cigarette case in murmuring meditation, but it is not always as it seems. Who has the most matches?
THE CALUMET OF PEACE
He offered a cigarette to the professor and took one himself. Lenehan promptly struck a match for them and lit their cigarettes in turn. J. J. O'Molloy opened his case again and offered it.
—_Thanky vous_, Lenehan said, helping himself.
The editor came from the inner office, a straw hat at an angle on his brow. He declaimed in song, pointing sternly at Professor MacHugh:

'Twas rank and fame that tempted thee,
     'Twas empire charmed thy heart.
The professor grinned, pressing his long lips together.
—Eh? You bloody old Roman Empire? Myles Crawford said.
He took a cigarette from the open case. Lenehan, lighting it for him with quick grace, said:
—Silence for my brand-new riddle!
—_Imperium Romanum_, J. J. O'Molloy said gently. It sounds nobler than British or Brixton. The word somehow reminds one of fat in the fire.
Myles Crawford blew his first puff violently towards the ceiling.
—That's it, he said. We are the fat. You and I are the fat in the fire. We haven't got a snowball's chance in hell.
THE GRANDEUR THAT WAS ROME
—Wait a moment, Professor MacHugh said, raising two quiet claw-like hands. We mustn't be led astray by words, by the sounds of words. We think of Rome: imperial, imperious, imperative.
He extended oratorical arms from frayed, stained shirt cuffs, pausing:

—What was their civilisation? Vast, I grant you: but vile. Cloacae: sewers. The Jews in the wilderness and on the mountaintop said: _It is fitting to be here. Let us build an altar to Jehovah._ The Roman, like the Englishman who follows in his footsteps, brought to every new shore on which he set foot — our shore he never set foot on — only his obsession with plumbing. He looked around him in his toga and said: _It is fitting to be here. Let us construct a toilet._
—Which they duly did, Lenehan said. Our ancient ancestors, as we read in the first chapter of Guinness's history, preferred the running stream.
—They were nature's gentlemen, J. J. O'Molloy murmured. But we also have Roman law.
—And Pontius Pilate is its prophet, Professor MacHugh responded.
—Do you know that story about Chief Baron Palles? J. J. O'Molloy asked. It was at the Royal University dinner. Everything was going swimmingly...
—First my riddle, Lenehan said. Are you ready?
Mr O'Madden Burke, tall in a generous suit of grey Donegal tweed, came in from the hallway. Stephen Dedalus, behind him, bare-headed as he entered.
—_Come in, children!_ Lenehan cried.
—I escort a supplicant, Mr O'Madden Burke said melodiously. Youth led by Experience visits Notoriety.
—How do you do? the editor said, holding out a hand. Come in. Your father just left.
Lenehan said to all:
—Silence! What opera resembles a railway line? Reflect, ponder, think it over, reply.
Stephen handed over the typed sheets, pointing to the title and signature.
—Who? the editor asked.
A bit torn off.
—Mr Garrett Deasy, Stephen said.
—That old tightwad, the editor said. Who tore it? Did he have a sudden need for the toilet?

On swift sail flaming
     From storm and south
     He comes, pale vampire,
     Mouth to my mouth.
—Good day, Stephen, the professor said, coming to peer over their shoulders. Foot and mouth disease? Are you turning into...?
The cattle-befriending poet.
SHINDY IN WELLKNOWN RESTAURANT
—Good day, sir, Stephen answered, blushing. The letter is not mine. Mr Garrett Deasy asked me to...

—Oh, I know him, Myles Crawford said, and I knew his wife too. The bloodiest old harridan God ever made. By Jesus, she had foot-and-mouth disease and no mistake! The night she threw the soup in the waiter's face at the Star and Garter. Oho!
A woman brought sin into the world. For Helen, the runaway wife of Menelaus, ten years the Greeks fought. O'Rourke, prince of Breffni.
—Is he a widower? Stephen asked.

—Well, as good as, Myles Crawford said, his eye running down the typescript. Emperor's horses. Habsburg. An Irishman saved the emperor's life on the ramparts of Vienna. Don't forget that! Maximilian Karl O'Donnell, Count von Tirconnell in Ireland. Sent his heir over to make the king an Austrian field marshal now. There's going to be trouble there one day. Wild Geese — Irish soldiers abroad. Oh yes, every time. Don't you forget that!
—The real question is whether the emperor forgot it, J. J. O'Molloy said quietly, turning a horseshoe paperweight. Saving princes is a thankless job.
Professor MacHugh turned on him.
—And if he didn't? he said.
—I'll tell you how it happened, Myles Crawford began. There was a Hungarian one day...
LOST CAUSES NOBLE MARQUESS MENTIONED

—We were always loyal to lost causes, the professor said. Success for us is the death of the intellect and of the imagination. We were never loyal to the successful. We serve them. I teach the blunt Latin language. I speak the tongue of a race whose highest wisdom is the maxim: time is money. Material domination. _Dominus!_ Lord! Where is the spirituality? Lord Jesus? Lord Salisbury? A sofa in a West End club. But the Greek!
KYRIE ELEISON!
A smile of light brightened his dark-rimmed eyes, lengthened his long lips.

—The Greek! he said again. _Kyrios!_ Shining word! The vowels that neither the Semite nor the Saxon know. _Kyrie!_ The radiance of the intellect. I ought to be a professor of Greek, the language of the mind. _Kyrie eleison!_ — Lord, have mercy! The toilet-maker and the sewer-builder will never be lords of our spirit. We are loyal subjects of the Catholic chivalry of Europe that went down at Trafalgar and of the empire of the spirit — not a material _imperium_ — that went down with the Athenian fleets at Aegospotami. Yes, yes. They went under. Pyrrhus, misled by an oracle, made a last attempt to restore the fortunes of Greece. Loyal to a lost cause.
He strode away from them towards the window.
—They went forth to battle, Mr O'Madden Burke said grimly, but they always fell.
—Boohoo! Lenehan wept with a little noise. Hit by a brick in the second half. Poor, poor, poor Pyrrhus!
He whispered then near Stephen's ear:
LENEHAN'S LIMERICK

—_There's a ponderous pundit MacHugh
Who wears goggles of ebony hue.
As he mostly sees double
To wear them why trouble?
I can't see the joke. Can you?_
In mourning for the Roman historian Sallust, Mulligan says. Whose mother is completely dead.
Myles Crawford crammed the sheets into a side pocket.
—That'll be all right, he said. I'll read the rest later. That'll be all right.
Lenehan extended his hands in protest.
—But my riddle! he said. What opera is like a railway line?
—Opera? Mr O'Madden Burke's sphinx-like face re-riddled.
Lenehan announced gladly:
—_The Rose of Castile_. See the joke? Rows of cast steel. Ha!
He poked Mr O'Madden Burke mildly in the ribs. Mr O'Madden Burke fell back gracefully on his umbrella, feigning a gasp.
—Help! he sighed. I feel a strong weakness.
Lenehan, rising on tiptoe, fanned his face rapidly with the rustling racing pages.
The professor, returning past the files, swept his hand across Stephen's and Mr O'Madden Burke's loose ties.
—Paris, past and present, he said. You look like French revolutionaries.

—Like fellows who had blown up the Bastille, J. J. O'Molloy said with quiet mockery. Or was it you two who shot the governor-general of Finland? You look as though you had done the deed. General Bobrikoff.
OMNIUM GATHERUM
—We were only thinking about it, Stephen said.
—All the talents gathered here, Myles Crawford said. Law, the classics...
—Horse racing, Lenehan put in.
—Literature, the press.
—If Bloom were here, the professor said. The gentle art of advertising.
—And Madam Bloom, Mr O'Madden Burke added. The vocal muse. Dublin's favourite singer.
Lenehan gave a loud cough.
—Ahem! he said very softly. Oh, for a breath of fresh air! I caught a cold in the park. The gate was open.
"YOU CAN DO IT!"
The editor laid a nervous hand on Stephen's shoulder.
—I want you to write something for me, he said. Something with a bite to it. You can do it. I see it in your face. _In the lexicon of youth_...
See it in your face. See it in your eye. Lazy, idle little schemer.

—Foot-and-mouth disease! the editor cried scornfully. Great nationalist meeting in Borris-in-Ossory. All rubbish! Hoodwinking the public! Give them something with a bite to it. Put us all into it, damn it all. Father, Son and Holy Ghost and Jakes McCarthy.
—We can all supply intellectual nourishment, Mr O'Madden Burke said.
Stephen raised his eyes to the bold, unseeing stare.
—He wants to press-gang you, J. J. O'Molloy said.
THE GREAT GALLAHER

—You can do it, Myles Crawford repeated, clenching his fist for emphasis. Wait a minute. We'll paralyse Europe, as Ignatius Gallaher used to say when he was down on his luck, marking billiards at the Clarence Hotel. Gallaher — now there was a pressman for you. That was a pen. You know how he made his name? I'll tell you. That was the smartest piece of journalism ever known. That was in eighty-one, sixth of May, the time of the Invincibles — the murder in the Phoenix Park — before you were born, I suppose. I'll show you.
He pushed past them to the files.
—Look at this, he said, turning. The _New York World_ cabled for a special report. Remember that time?
Professor MacHugh nodded.

—_New York World_, the editor said, excitedly pushing back his straw hat. Where the murder took place. Tim Kelly — or Kavanagh, I mean. Joe Brady and the rest of them. Where Skin-the-Goat drove the getaway car. The whole route, see?
—Skin-the-Goat, Mr O'Madden Burke said. Fitzharris. He has that cabman's shelter, they say, down at Butt Bridge. Holohan told me. You know Holohan?
—The one who limps, is it? Myles Crawford said.
—And poor Gumley is down there too, he told me, guarding stones for the city council. A night watchman.
Stephen turned in surprise.
—Gumley? he said. You don't say so? A friend of my father's, is it?

—Never mind Gumley, Myles Crawford cried angrily. Let Gumley mind the stones, make sure they don't run away. Look at this. What did Ignatius Gallaher do? I'll tell you. A stroke of genius. Cabled the story right away. Have you got the _Weekly Freeman_ of 17 March? Right. Have you got that?
He flung back pages of the files and stuck his finger on a point.
—Take page four, an advertisement for Bransome's coffee, let us say. Have you got that? Right.
The telephone whirred.
A DISTANT VOICE
—I'll answer it, the professor said, going.
—B is Parkgate. Good.
His finger leaped and struck point after point, vibrating.
—T is the Viceregal Lodge. C is where the murder took place. K is Knockmaroon Gate.
The loose flesh of his neck shook like a rooster's wattles. A badly starched shirt-front jutted up and with a rude gesture he thrust it back into his waistcoat.
—Hello? _Evening Telegraph_ here... Hello?... Who's there?... Yes... Yes... Yes.
—F to P is the route Skin-the-Goat drove the car as an alibi: Inchicore, Roundtown, Windy Arbour, Palmerston Park, Ranelagh. F.A.B.P. Got that? X is Davy's pub in upper Leeson Street.
The professor came to the inner door.
—Bloom is on the telephone, he said.
—Tell him to go to hell, the editor said promptly. X is Davy's pub, see?
CLEVER, VERY
—Clever, Lenehan said. Very.
—Gave it to them on a hot plate, Myles Crawford said, the whole bloody history.
A nightmare from which you will never awake.
—I saw it happen, the editor said proudly. I was there. Dick Adams, the best-hearted bloody Corkman the Lord ever breathed life into, and myself.
Lenehan bowed to an imaginary figure, announcing:
—Madam, I'm Adam. And: Able was I ere I saw Elba.

—History! Myles Crawford cried. The Old Woman of Prince's Street — our paper — was there first. There was weeping and gnashing of teeth over that scoop. All from an advertisement. Gregor Grey designed the layout. That gave Gallaher his break. Then Paddy Hooper got him work with T.P. O'Connor, who took him on at the _Star_. Now he's in with Blumenfeld at the _Daily Express_. That's journalism. That's talent. Pyatt! Gallaher was the daddy of them all!
—The father of sensationalist journalism, Lenehan confirmed, and the brother-in-law of Chris Callinan.
—Hello?... Are you there?... Yes, he's still here. Come across yourself.
—Where do you find a pressman like that nowadays, eh? the editor cried.
He flung the pages down.
—Damn clever, Lenehan said to Mr O'Madden Burke.
—Very smart, Mr O'Madden Burke said.
Professor MacHugh came from the inner office.
—Speaking of the Invincibles, he said, did you see that some street hawkers were up before the judge...

—Oh yes, J. J. O'Molloy said eagerly. Lady Dudley was walking home through the Phoenix Park to see all the trees that were blown down by that cyclone last year, and she thought she'd buy a view of Dublin from one of them. And it turned out to be a commemorative postcard of Joe Brady or Number One or Skin-the-Goat. Right outside the Viceregal Lodge, imagine!

—They're small-time operators, Myles Crawford said. Pah! The press and the bar! Where have you a man now at the bar like those fellows — like Whiteside, like Isaac Butt, like silver-tongued O'Hagan? Eh? Ah, bloody nonsense. Pah! Today's lot are nothing.
His mouth continued to twitch silently in nervous curls of disdain.
Would anyone wish that mouth for her kiss? How do you know? Why did you write it then?
RHYMES AND REASONS
Mouth, south. Is the mouth south somehow? Or the south a mouth? There must be some connection. South, pout, out, shout, drought. Rhymes: two men dressed the same, looking the same, two by two.

........................ la tua pace
     .................. che parlar ti piace
     Mentre che il vento, come fa, si tace.

He saw them three by three, approaching girls, in green, in rose, in russet, intertwining, _through the dark air_, in mauve, in purple, _that peaceful banner of flame_, gold of the oriflamme, _making those who behold it burn with greater ardour_. But I, old man, penitent, leaden-footed, underneath the night: mouth south: tomb womb.
—Speak up for yourself, Mr O'Madden Burke said.
SUFFICIENT FOR THE DAY...
J. J. O'Molloy, smiling palely, took up the challenge.

—My dear Myles, he said, flinging his cigarette aside, you put a false construction on my words. I hold no brief, as it stands, for the legal profession as such, but your Cork enthusiasm is running away with you. Why not bring in Henry Grattan and Flood and Demosthenes and Edmund Burke? We all know Ignatius Gallaher and his Chapelizod boss, Harmsworth of the penny press, and his American cousin of the Bowery gutter-sheet — not to mention _Paddy Kelly's Budget_, _Pue's Occurrences_, and our watchful friend _The Skibbereen Eagle_. Why bring in a master of courtroom eloquence like Whiteside? Sufficient for the day is the newspaper thereof.
LINKS WITH BYGONE DAYS OF YORE
—Grattan and Flood wrote for this very paper, the editor cried in his face. Irish Volunteers. Where are you now? Established 1763. Dr Lucas. Who have you now like John Philpot Curran? Pah!
—Well, J. J. O'Molloy said, Bushe K.C., for example.
—Bushe? the editor said. Well, yes: Bushe, yes. He has a strain of it in his blood. Kendal Bushe — or I mean Seymour Bushe.
—He would have been on the bench long ago, the professor said, only for... But no matter.
J. J. O'Molloy turned to Stephen and said quietly and slowly:
—One of the most polished pieces of oratory I think I ever heard in my life fell from the lips of Seymour Bushe. It was in that fratricide case, the Childs murder case. Bushe was the defence.
_And in the porches of mine ear did pour._
By the way, how did he find that out? The man died in his sleep. Or the other story — the beast with two backs?
—What was that? the professor asked.
ITALIA, MAGISTRA ARTIUM

—He spoke on the law of evidence, J. J. O'Molloy said, on Roman justice as contrasted with the earlier Mosaic code, the law of an eye for an eye. And he cited the Moses of Michelangelo in the Vatican.
—Ha.
—A few well-chosen words, Lenehan said by way of introduction. Silence!
Pause. J. J. O'Molloy took out his cigarette case.
False lull. Something quite ordinary.
The man took out his matchbox thoughtfully and lit his cigar.
I have often thought since, looking back over that strange time, that it was that small act, trivial in itself — the striking of that match — that determined the whole course of both our lives.
A POLISHED PERIOD
J. J. O'Molloy resumed, shaping his words carefully:

—He said of it: _that stony effigy in frozen music, horned and terrible, of the human form divine, that eternal symbol of wisdom and prophecy which, if anything that the imagination or the hand of sculptor has wrought in marble of soul-transfigured and soul-transfiguring stone deserves to live, deserves to live._
His slim hand waved gracefully, echoing the rise and fall.
—Fine! Myles Crawford said at once.
—The divine inspiration, Mr O'Madden Burke said.
—You like it? J. J. O'Molloy asked Stephen.

Stephen, his blood stirred by the grace of the language and gesture, blushed. He took a cigarette from the case. J. J. O'Molloy offered his case to Myles Crawford. Lenehan lit their cigarettes as before and took his reward, saying:
—Many thankibus.
A MAN OF HIGH MORALE

—Professor Magennis was speaking to me about you, J. J. O'Molloy said to Stephen. What do you really think of that mystical crowd, the dreamy poets: A.E. the master mystic? That Blavatsky woman started the whole thing. She was a fine old bag of tricks. A.E. has been telling some American interviewer that you came to him in the small hours of the morning to ask him about planes of consciousness. Magennis thinks you must have been pulling A.E.'s leg. Magennis is a man of the very highest moral standards.
Speaking about me. What did he say? What did he say? What did he say about me? Don't ask.

—No thanks, Professor MacHugh said, waving the cigarette case aside. Wait a moment. Let me say one thing. The finest display of oratory I ever heard was a speech made by John F. Taylor at the College Historical Society. Mr Justice Fitzgibbon, the present Lord Justice of Appeal, had spoken, and the paper under debate was an essay — new for those days — advocating the revival of the Irish language.
He turned towards Myles Crawford and said:
—You know Gerald Fitzgibbon. Then you can imagine the style of his speech.
—He is sitting alongside Tim Healy, J. J. O'Molloy said — rumour has it — on the Trinity College estates commission.
—He is sitting with a young thing, Myles Crawford said, in a child's frock. Go on. Well?

—It was the speech, mark you, the professor said, of a polished orator, full of courteous arrogance, and pouring in refined language — I will not say the vials of his wrath but pouring the proud man's contempt upon the new movement. It was then a new movement. We were weak, therefore worthless.

He closed his long thin lips for an instant but, eager to continue, raised an outstretched hand to his spectacles and, with trembling thumb and ring finger touching lightly the black rims, steadied them to a new focus.
IMPROMPTU
In a solemn, weekday tone, he addressed J. J. O'Molloy:

—Taylor had come there, you must know, from a sickbed. That he had prepared his speech I do not believe, for there was not even one shorthand writer in the hall. His dark lean face had a growth of shaggy beard around it. He wore a loose white silk necktie, and altogether he looked — though he was not — a dying man.

His gaze turned at once but slowly from J. J. O'Molloy's face towards Stephen's and then bent at once to the ground, searching. His unstarched linen collar appeared behind his bent head, soiled by his thinning hair. Still searching, he said:
—When Fitzgibbon's speech had ended, John F. Taylor rose to reply. Briefly, as well as I can recall, his words were these.
He raised his head firmly. His eyes gathered themselves once more. Vague, swimming shapes moved behind the thick lenses, back and forth, seeking a way out.
He began:

_—Mr Chairman, ladies and gentlemen: Great was my admiration in listening to the remarks addressed to the youth of Ireland a moment ago by my learned friend. It seemed to me that I had been transported to a country far away from this country, into an age remote from this age — that I stood in ancient Egypt and that I was listening to the speech of some high priest of that land addressed to the youthful Moses._

His listeners held their cigarettes poised to hear, their smoke ascending in frail stalks that bloomed with his speech. _And let our crooked smokes_ — noble words coming. Watch out. Could you try your hand at it yourself?
_—And it seemed to me that I heard the voice of that Egyptian high priest raised in a tone of equal arrogance and equal pride. I heard his words and their meaning was revealed to me._
FROM THE FATHERS
It was revealed to me that those things are good which yet are corrupted, which neither if they were supremely good nor unless they were good could be corrupted. Ah, damn it! That's Saint Augustine.

_—Why will you Jews not accept our culture, our religion, and our language? You are a tribe of nomad herdsmen: we are a mighty people. You have no cities nor wealth: our cities are hives of humanity and our galleys, with three and four banks of oars, laden with all manner of merchandise, furrow the waters of the known world. You have barely emerged from primitive conditions: we have a literature, a priesthood, an age-old history, and a system of government._
Nile.
Child, man, effigy.
By the banks of the Nile the holy mothers kneel, cradle of bulrushes: a man supple in combat: stone-horned, stone-bearded, heart of stone.

_—You pray to a local and obscure idol: our temples, majestic and mysterious, are the abodes of Isis and Osiris, of Horus and Ammon Ra. Yours is serfdom, awe, and humbleness: ours is thunder and the seas. Israel is weak and few are her children: Egypt is a host and terrible are her arms. Vagrants and day-labourers you are called: the world trembles at our name._
A silent belch of hunger broke through his speech. He raised his voice above it boldly:

_—But, ladies and gentlemen, had the youthful Moses listened to and accepted that view of life, had he bowed his head and bowed his will and bowed his spirit before that arrogant warning, he would never have brought the chosen people out of their house of bondage, nor followed the pillar of cloud by day. He would never have spoken with the Eternal amid lightning on Sinai's mountaintop, nor ever have come down with the light of inspiration shining in his face and bearing in his arms the tablets of the law, graven in the language of the outcast._
He stopped and looked at them, enjoying the silence.
OMINOUS — FOR HIM!
J. J. O'Molloy said, not without regret:
—And yet he died without having entered the promised land.
—A-sudden-at-the-moment-though-from-lingering-illness-often-previously-expected-demise, Lenehan added. And with a great future behind him.
The troop of bare feet was heard rushing along the hallway and pattering up the staircase.
—That is oratory, the professor said, and no one contradicted him.

Gone with the wind. The great gatherings at Mullaghmast and Tara of the Kings. Miles and miles of listening ears. The speaker's words, howled and scattered to the four winds. A people sheltered within his voice. Dead noise. Eternal records of all that ever anywhere wherever was. Love and praise him: me no more.
I have money.
—Gentlemen, Stephen said. As the next motion on the agenda, may I suggest that the house now adjourn?
—You take my breath away. Is this perhaps a French compliment? Mr O'Madden Burke asked. It is the hour, I think, when a drink, metaphorically speaking, is most welcome in the ancient pub.
—That it be and hereby is resolutely resolved. All in favour say aye, Lenehan announced. The contrary, no. I declare it carried. To which particular drinking hole...? My casting vote is: Mooney's!
He led the way, admonishing:
—We will sternly refuse to partake of strong drink, will we not? Yes, we will not. By no means whatsoever.
Mr O'Madden Burke, following close behind, said with an ally's thrust of his umbrella:
—Lead on, Macduff!
—Chip of the old block! the editor cried, clapping Stephen on the shoulder. Let us go. Where are those damned keys?
He fumbled in his pocket, pulling out the crushed typed sheets.
—Foot and mouth. I know. That'll be all right. That'll go in. Where are they? That's all right.
He thrust the sheets back and went into the inner office.
LET US HOPE
J. J. O'Molloy, about to follow him in, said quietly to Stephen:
—I hope you will live to see it published. Myles, one moment.
He went into the inner office, closing the door behind him.

—Come along, Stephen, the professor said. That was fine, wasn't it? It has prophetic vision. _Fuit Ilium!_ — Troy has fallen! Kingdoms of this world. The masters of the Mediterranean are peasants today.
The first newsboy came pattering down the stairs at their heels and rushed out into the street, yelling:
—Racing special!
Dublin. I have much, much to learn.
They turned left along Abbey Street.
—I have a vision too, Stephen said.
—Yes? the professor said, skipping to get into step. Crawford will follow.
Another newsboy shot past them, yelling as he ran:
—Racing special!
DEAR DIRTY DUBLIN
Dubliners.
—Two Dublin ladies, Stephen said, elderly and devout, have lived fifty and fifty-three years in Fumbally's Lane.
—Where is that? the professor asked.
—Off Blackpitts, Stephen said.
Damp night reeking of raw dough. Against the wall. Face glistening like tallow under her rough shawl. Racing hearts. Eternal records. Quicker, darling!
On now. Dare it. Let there be life.

—They want to see the views of Dublin from the top of Nelson's Pillar. They save up three shillings and tenpence in a red tin letter-box money box. They shake out the threepenny bits and sixpences and coax out the pennies with the blade of a knife. Two and three in silver and one and seven in copper. They put on their bonnets and best clothes and take their umbrellas in case it rains.
—Wise virgins, Professor MacHugh said.
LIFE ON THE RAW

—They buy one and fourpence worth of pressed meat and four slices of bread at the north city dining rooms in Marlborough Street from Miss Kate Collins, proprietress... They purchase twenty-four ripe plums from a girl at the foot of Nelson's Pillar to wash down the meat. They give two threepenny bits to the man at the turnstile and begin to waddle slowly up the winding staircase, grunting, encouraging each other, afraid of the dark, panting, one asking the other have you got the meat, praising God and the Blessed Virgin, threatening to come back down, peeping through the air slits. Glory be to God. They had no idea it was that high up.

Their names are Anne Kearns and Florence MacCabe. Anne Kearns has lumbago, for which she rubs on Lourdes water, given to her by a lady who got a whole bottleful from a Passionist father. Florence MacCabe has a pig's trotter and a bottle of extra-strong stout for supper every Saturday.
—Antithesis, the professor said, nodding twice. Vestal virgins. I can see them. What's keeping our friend?
He turned.

A crowd of scampering newsboys rushed down the steps, scattering in all directions, yelling, their white papers fluttering. Close behind them Myles Crawford appeared on the steps, his hat making a halo around his scarlet face, talking with J. J. O'Molloy.
—Come along, the professor cried, waving his arm.
He set off again to walk by Stephen's side.
RETURN OF BLOOM
—Yes, he said. I see them.
Mr Bloom, breathless, caught in a whirl of wild newsboys near the offices of the _Irish Catholic_ and _Dublin Penny Journal_, called:
—Mr Crawford! A moment!
—_Telegraph_! Racing special!
—What is it? Myles Crawford said, falling back a pace.
A newsboy cried in Mr Bloom's face:
—Terrible tragedy in Rathmines! A child bit by a bellows!
INTERVIEW WITH THE EDITOR

—Just this ad, Mr Bloom said, pushing through towards the steps, puffing, and taking the cutting from his pocket. I spoke with Mr Keyes just now. He'll give a renewal for two months, he says. After that he'll see. But he wants a paragraph calling attention to it in the _Telegraph_ too, the Saturday pink edition. And he wants it copied — if it's not too late — I told Councillor Nannetti, from the _Kilkenny People_. I can get access to it in the National Library. House of Keys, don't you see? His name is Keyes. It's a play on the name. But he practically promised he'd give the renewal. But he wants just a little puff. What should I tell him, Mr Crawford?
K.M.A.
—Will you tell him he can kiss my arse? Myles Crawford said, throwing out his arm for emphasis. Tell him that straight from the horse's mouth.

A bit on edge. Watch out for trouble. All heading off for a drink. Arm in arm. Lenehan's yachting cap — always scrounging. The usual blarney. I wonder if that young Dedalus is the ringleader. Has a good pair of boots on him today. Last time I saw him his heels were worn right through. Been walking through mud somewhere. Careless fellow. What was he doing in Irishtown?
—Well, Mr Bloom said, his eyes returning, if I can get the design I suppose it's worth a short paragraph. He'd give the ad, I think. I'll tell him...
K.M.R.I.A.
—He can kiss my royal Irish arse, Myles Crawford cried loudly over his shoulder. Any time he likes, tell him.
While Mr Bloom stood weighing the point and about to smile, the editor strode on jerkily.
RAISING THE WIND

—No money, Jack, he said, raising his hand to his chin. I'm up to here in debt. I've been through the wringer myself. I was looking for someone to co-sign a loan for me just last week. Sorry, Jack. You must take the will for the deed. With all my heart, if I could raise the cash somehow.
J. J. O'Molloy pulled a long face and walked on in silence. They caught up with the others and walked side by side.
—When they have eaten the pressed meat and the bread and wiped their twenty fingers in the paper the bread was wrapped in, they go closer to the railings.
—Something for you, the professor explained to Myles Crawford. Two old Dublin women on the top of Nelson's Pillar.
SOME COLUMN! — THAT'S WHAT WADDLER ONE SAID
—That's new, Myles Crawford said. That's copy. A day out at the seaside. Two old characters, what?

—But they are afraid the pillar will fall, Stephen went on. They see the roofs and argue about where the different churches are: Rathmines' blue dome, Adam and Eve's, Saint Laurence O'Toole's. But it makes them dizzy to look, so they pull up their skirts...
THOSE SLIGHTLY RAMBUNCTIOUS FEMALES
—Easy now, Myles Crawford said. No poetic licence. We're in the archbishop's territory here.
—And settle down on their striped petticoats, peering up at the statue of the one-handed adulterer.
—One-handed adulterer! the professor cried. I like that. I see the idea. I see what you mean.
DAMES DONATE DUBLIN'S CITS SPEEDPILLS VELOCITOUS AEROLITHS, BELIEF

—It gives them a crick in their necks, Stephen said, and they are too tired to look up or down or to speak. They put the bag of plums between them and eat the plums out of it, one after another, wiping off with their handkerchiefs the plum juice that dribbles out of their mouths and spitting the plum stones slowly out between the railings.
He gave a sudden loud young laugh as a finish. Lenehan and Mr O'Madden Burke, hearing, turned, beckoned, and led on across towards Mooney's pub.
—Finished? Myles Crawford said. So long as they do no worse.
SOPHIST WALLOPS HAUGHTY HELEN SQUARE ON PROBOSCIS. SPARTANS GNASH MOLARS. ITHACANS VOW PEN IS CHAMP.

—You remind me of Antisthenes, the professor said, a disciple of Gorgias the sophist. It is said of him that no one could tell if he was more bitter against others or against himself. He was the son of a nobleman and a slave-woman. And he wrote a book in which he took the prize for beauty away from Helen of Argos and gave it to poor Penelope.
Poor Penelope. Penelope Rich.
They made ready to cross O'Connell Street.
HELLO THERE, CENTRAL!

At various points along the eight tram lines, tramcars with motionless trolleys stood in their tracks, bound for or from Rathmines, Rathfarnham, Blackrock, Kingstown and Dalkey, Sandymount Green, Ringsend and Sandymount Tower, Donnybrook, Palmerston Park and Upper Rathmines — all still, becalmed in short circuit. Hackney cabs, hansom cabs, delivery wagons, mail vans, private carriages, mineral water floats with rattling crates of bottles — rattled, rolled, horse-drawn, rapidly.
WHAT? — AND LIKEWISE — WHERE?
—But what do you call it? Myles Crawford asked. Where did they get the plums?
